claim: At least 22.2% (about 5.4 million) of individuals over the age of 71 in the United States have at least mild cognitive impairment.
source: A 2008 study estimated that at least 22.2% (about 5.4 million) of individuals over the age of 71 in the United States have at least mild cognitive impairment (Plassman, 2008; Langa and Levine, 2014; Gillis et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies (Plassman, 2008; Langa and Levine, 2014; Gillis et al., 2019).

claim: Global dementia cases are predicted to triple from an estimated 57.4 million cases in 2019 to 152.8 million cases in 2050.
source: Furthermore, global dementia cases are predicted to triple from an estimated 57.4 million cases in 2019–152.8 million cases in 2050 (Feigin et al., 2020; Nichols and Vos, 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies (Feigin et al., 2020; Nichols and Vos, 2020).

claim: C. elegans has a simple nervous system.
source: C. elegans is an excellent model system for studying neuronal aging, given its tractable genetics, short lifespan, and simple nervous system (White et al., 1986).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to White et al., 1986, which is a foundational reference for C. elegans nervous system anatomy.

claim: By Day 4 of adulthood, all long-term associative memory ability is lost in C. elegans.
source: by Day 4 of adulthood, all long-term associative memory ability is lost, and by Day 8, C. elegans cannot carry out associative learning or short-term associative memory (Kauffman et al., 2010)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kauffman et al., 2010.

claim: By Day 8 of adulthood, C. elegans cannot carry out associative learning or short-term associative memory.
source: by Day 4 of adulthood, all long-term associative memory ability is lost, and by Day 8, C. elegans cannot carry out associative learning or short-term associative memory (Kauffman et al., 2010)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kauffman et al., 2010.

claim: With age, C. elegans worms first lose long-term memory ability (by Day 4), then short-term memory and learning ability (Day 6–8), then chemotaxis (Day 10–12), then motility (Day 16).
source: That is, with age worms first lose long-term memory ability (by Day 4), then short-term memory and learning ability (Day 6–8), then chemotaxis (Day 10–12), then motility (Day 16) (Kauffman et al., 2010; Hahm et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kauffman et al., 2010 and Hahm et al., 2015.

claim: The lifespan of daf-2/Insulin/IGF-1 receptor mutants is twice that of wild-type animals.
source: The lifespan of daf-2/Insulin/IGF-1 receptor mutants is twice that of wild-type animals (Kenyon et al., 1993)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kenyon et al., 1993.

claim: The lifespan extension of daf-2 mutants requires the downstream Forkhead box O (FOXO) transcription factor DAF-16.
source: this lifespan extension requires the downstream Forkhead box O (FOXO) transcription factor DAF-16 (Kenyon et al., 1993).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kenyon et al., 1993.

claim: DAF-16/FOXO controls the expression of many genes that contribute to longevity, including stress response, proteostasis, autophagy, antimicrobial, and metabolic genes.
source: DAF-16/FOXO controls the expression of many genes that contribute to longevity, including stress response, proteostasis, autophagy, antimicrobial, and metabolic genes (Murphy et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Murphy et al., 2003.

claim: The IIS/FOXO pathway regulates longevity in Drosophila, mice, and humans.
source: As a conserved regulator, the IIS/FOXO pathway also regulates longevity in Drosophila, mice, and humans (Clancy et al., 2001; Blüher et al., 2003; Suh et al., 2008; Willcox et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies (Clancy et al., 2001; Blüher et al., 2003; Suh et al., 2008; Willcox et al., 2008).

claim: C. elegans IIS/daf-2 mutants display DAF-16-dependent improved learning, short-term memory, and long-term memory.
source: In particular, C. elegans IIS/daf-2 mutants display DAF-16-dependent improved learning, short-term memory, and long-term memory (Kauffman et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kauffman et al., 2010.

claim: Compared to wild-type worms, daf-2 mutants better maintain maximum velocity with age.
source: Compared to wild-type worms, daf-2 mutants better maintain maximum velocity (Hahm et al., 2015)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hahm et al., 2015.

claim: daf-2 mutants better maintain motility with age compared to wild-type worms.
source: Compared to wild-type worms, daf-2 mutants better maintain maximum velocity (Hahm et al., 2015), motility (Liu et al., 2013; Li et al., 2016)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Liu et al., 2013 and Li et al., 2016.

claim: daf-2 mutants better maintain neuromuscular junctions with age compared to wild-type worms.
source: Compared to wild-type worms, daf-2 mutants better maintain maximum velocity (Hahm et al., 2015), motility (Liu et al., 2013; Li et al., 2016), neuromuscular junctions, the ability to regenerate axons (Byrne et al., 2014; Lakhina et al., 2019)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Byrne et al., 2014 and Lakhina et al., 2019.

claim: daf-2 mutants better maintain the ability to regenerate axons with age compared to wild-type worms.
source: Compared to wild-type worms, daf-2 mutants better maintain maximum velocity (Hahm et al., 2015), motility (Liu et al., 2013; Li et al., 2016), neuromuscular junctions, the ability to regenerate axons (Byrne et al., 2014; Lakhina et al., 2019)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Byrne et al., 2014 and Lakhina et al., 2019.

claim: daf-2 mutants better maintain neuronal morphology with age compared to wild-type worms.
source: Compared to wild-type worms, daf-2 mutants better maintain maximum velocity (Hahm et al., 2015), motility (Liu et al., 2013; Li et al., 2016), neuromuscular junctions, the ability to regenerate axons (Byrne et al., 2014; Lakhina et al., 2019), and neuronal morphology with age (Pan et al., 2011; Tank et al., 2011; Toth et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Pan et al., 2011; Tank et al., 2011; and Toth et al., 2012.

claim: daf-2 has lower observed motility on food.
source: In particular, we previously showed that while daf-2 has lower observed motility on food (Bansal et al., 2015)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bansal et al., 2015.

claim: The apparent lower motility of daf-2 on food is due to its high levels of a food receptor, ODR-10.
source: this apparent is due to its high levels of a food receptor, ODR-10 (Hahm et al., 2015)

claim: Downregulation of ODR-10 reveals the much higher mobility of daf-2 animals.
source: and its downregulation reveals the much higher mobility of daf-2 animals (Hahm et al., 2015)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hahm et al., 2015.

claim: daf-2 worms extend learning beyond the wild-type's ability.
source: Previously, we found that daf-2 worms also extend learning beyond the wild-type's ability (Kauffman et al., 2010)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kauffman et al., 2010.

claim: Neuron-specific targets were identified in young (Day 1) adult C. elegans through neuron-specific RNA-sequencing.
source: We previously performed neuron-specific RNA-sequencing in young (Day 1) adult C. elegans and identified neuron-specific targets (Kaletsky et al., 2016)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kaletsky et al., 2016.

claim: Genes upregulated in daf-2 mutant neurons are distinct from those in the whole animal.
source: genes upregulated in daf-2 mutant neurons are distinct from those in the whole animal, and we found that these neuronal genes are necessary for the observed improvements in memory and axon regeneration in daf-2 mutant worms.
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' previous work (Kaletsky et al., 2016) as referenced in the preceding sentence.

claim: Neuronal genes upregulated in daf-2 mutants are necessary for the observed improvements in memory and axon regeneration in daf-2 mutant worms.
source: genes upregulated in daf-2 mutant neurons are distinct from those in the whole animal, and we found that these neuronal genes are necessary for the observed improvements in memory and axon regeneration in daf-2 mutant worms.
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' previous work (Kaletsky et al., 2016) as referenced in the preceding sentence.

claim: Recent datasets using whole-animal single-cell RNA-seq have been generated for wild-type and daf-2 worms.
source: Recent datasets using whole-animal single-cell RNA-seq have been generated for wild-type and daf-2 worms, and these are sufficient for whole-body aging and pseudobulk analyses (Gao et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2022; Roux et al., 2023)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Gao et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2022; and Roux et al., 2023.

claim: Whole-animal single-cell RNA-seq data are not deep enough for in-depth analysis of neurons.
source: but we have found that those data are not deep enough to use specifically for in-depth analysis of neurons, which can be difficult to gather from whole animals.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' assessment of existing datasets (Gao et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2022; Roux et al., 2023).

claim: Wild-type worms lose their learning and short-term memory abilities by Day 7 of adulthood.
source: Adult Day 1 worms are fully developed, young, and healthy, while wild-type Day 7–8 worms, although still in their mid-life, have completely lost their learning and short-term memory abilities already by Day 7 (Kauffman et al., 2010; Figure 1a)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kauffman et al., 2010 and reference to Figure 1a.

claim: Wild-type Day 7-8 worms have completely lost their learning and short-term memory abilities.
source: Adult Day 1 worms are fully developed, young, and healthy, while wild-type Day 7–8 worms, although still in their mid-life, have completely lost their learning and short-term memory abilities already by Day 7 (Kauffman et al., 2010; Figure 1a)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kauffman et al., 2010 and reference to Figure 1a showing learning and memory results on Day 1 and Day 7.

claim: Over 99.94% of the cells collected by FACS are GFP+ neurons.
source: Over 99.94% of the cells collected are GFP + neurons.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text of Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and supported by FACS results shown in panels a-b.

claim: 100,000 cells are collected for each biological replicate.
source: 100,000 cells are collected for each biological replicate, six biological replicates for each condition.

claim: Six biological replicates were collected for each condition.

claim: An average of 41,636,463 uniquely-counted reads were obtained from the neuron RNA-seq samples.

claim: Genes declining with age in neurons encode proteins important in neuronal function, including synaptic proteins, potassium channels, and transmembrane transporters.
source: Gene ontology (GO) analysis suggested that genes declining with age in neurons encode proteins important in neuronal function (Figure 1e and f), including synaptic proteins (e.g. srh-59, rab-3, sng-1, sup-1), potassium channels (e.g. egl-23, twk-7, twk-49, ncs-5), and transmembrane transporters (e.g. folt-2, ccb-2, unc-79, exp-1).

claim: ins-6 regulates aversive learning.

evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Chen et al., 2013.

source: ins-6, an insulin-like peptide specific to the ASI, ASJ, and AWA neurons (Taylor et al., 2021) that regulates longevity (Artan et al., 2016) and aversive learning (Chen et al., 2013), is significantly downregulated with age (Figure 1g).

evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lakhina et al., 2019.

source: Previous studies showed that loss of genes including ins-6 (Chen et al., 2013), mec-7 (Savage et al., 1989), unc-4, folt-2 (Lakhina et al., 2019), madd-4 (Maro et al., 2015), and fbf-1 (Stein and Murphy, 2014) lead to behavioral dysfunction in motility and chemosensory abilities
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Stein and Murphy, 2014.

source: Specifically, 36 of the top 100 upregulated genes have identified orthologs or identified domains with known functions, of which 32 of (89%) have functions in promoting neuronal health.

claim: The reduction of F08H9.4 significantly decreased daf-2's learning ability on Day 6.

claim: The reduction of mtl-1 significantly decreased daf-2's learning ability on Day 6.

evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4d.

claim: The reduction of dod-24 significantly decreased daf-2's learning ability on Day 6.

claim: daf-2 mutants maintain learning and memory abilities proportional with (or even slightly beyond) their degree of lifespan extension.

evidence: The claim is supported by the behavioral data shown in Figure 3c-d and lifespan data, with reference to Hahm et al., 2015.

claim: Wild-type neuronal aging is characterized by a downregulation of neuronal function genes.
source: We found that wild-type neuronal aging is characterized by a downregulation of neuronal function genes and an upregulation of proteolysis genes and transcriptional and epigenetic regulators, which together may help explain the loss of neuronal identity and function with age.
evidence: The claim is supported by the RNA-seq data analysis of Day 1 vs Day 8 wild-type neurons shown in Figure 1.

claim: Wild-type neuronal aging is characterized by an upregulation of proteolysis genes and transcriptional and epigenetic regulators.
source: We found that wild-type neuronal aging is characterized by a downregulation of neuronal function genes and an upregulation of proteolysis genes and transcriptional and epigenetic regulators, which together may help explain the loss of neuronal identity and function with age.
evidence: The claim is supported by the RNA-seq data analysis of Day 1 vs Day 8 wild-type neurons shown in Figure 2.

claim: daf-2 neurons maintain higher expression of stress response genes.
source: Specifically, daf-2 neurons maintain higher expression of stress response genes and predicted neuronal homeostasis functions (Table 1), which may help make them more resistant to environmental adversities and age-related decline.
evidence: The claim is supported by the RNA-seq data analysis of Day 8 daf-2 vs daf-16;daf-2 neurons shown in Figure 3f and Table 1.

claim: dod-24 has been shown to be an innate immunity gene upregulated during pathogen infection.

claim: utx-1 is an H3K27me3 histone demethylase.

source: We found that the insulin-like peptide ins-19 was upregulated in aged neurons and was downregulated in aged daf-2 neurons, and its downregulation in wild-type worms extended memory span.
evidence: The claim is supported by the behavioral data shown in Figure 2f.

claim: Insulin-like peptides ins-7 and ins-18 are downregulated in daf-2 mutants compared with daf-16;daf-2 mutants.
source: we have found them to be downregulated in daf-2 mutants compared with daf-16;daf-2 mutants, possibly creating a feedback loop that dampens the insulin signaling pathway, as was previously shown for ins-7 and ins-18 (Murphy et al., 2003; Murphy et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Murphy et al., 2003 and Murphy et al., 2007.

claim: Insulin-like peptides exhibit diverse functions in development, dauer formation, and longevity.
source: These peptides exhibit diverse functions in development, dauer formation, and longevity (Murphy et al., 2003; Murphy et al., 2007; Thomé-Duret et al., 1998; Kawano et al., 2000; Pierce et al., 2001; Li et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies (Murphy et al., 2003; Murphy et al., 2007; Thomé-Duret et al., 1998; Kawano et al., 2000; Pierce et al., 2001; Li et al., 2003).

claim: ins-6 and ins-7 are two antagonistic peptides that regulate aversive learning.
source: Notably, certain insulin-like peptides have been linked to neuronal activities, such as the regulation of aversive learning by the two antagonistic peptides ins-6 and ins-7 (Chen et al., 2013)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Chen et al., 2013.

claim: ins-22 RNAi reduces long-term learning and memory.
source: and reduced long-term learning and memory by ins-22 RNAi (Lakhina et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lakhina et al., 2015.

claim: Wild-type neurons lose their neuronal identity through a combination of the loss of neuron-specific function genes with age and the concomitant dysregulated increase in non-neuronal genes with age.
source: Specifically, we found that wild-type neurons lose their neuronal identity through a combination of the loss of neuron-specific function genes with age, and the concomitant dysregulated increase in non-neuronal genes with age.
evidence: The claim is based on the RNA-seq data analysis of aging wild-type neurons shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: At least a fraction of the top-upregulated genes with age can play deleterious roles.
source: Furthermore, at least a fraction of the top-upregulated genes with age can play deleterious roles; that is, they rise with age, and their knockdown improves function, even in young animals.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data showing that knockdown of utx-1, ins-19, and nmgp-1 improves memory in young animals (Figure 2d, f, h).

claim: The knockdown of individual top-ranked genes that function in learning and memory can have a large impact.
source: We also found that the knockdown of individual top-ranked genes that function in learning and memory can have a large impact - like removing a cog of a machine.
evidence: The claim is based on the experimental data showing significant effects of individual gene knockdowns on learning and memory (Figure 4d-e).

claim: Loss of individual major genes downstream of DAF-2 and DAF-16 have at most a 5–10% impact on lifespan.
source: This is in contrast to our earlier findings regarding gene reduction in lifespan, where most cellular longevity processes regulated by DAF-16 activity appear to be additive, and therefore loss of individual major genes downstream of DAF-2 and DAF-16 have at most a 5–10% impact (White et al., 1986; Murphy et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to White et al., 1986 and Murphy et al., 2003.

claim: dod-24, F08H9.4, C44B7.5, and alh-2 were previously not associated with memory function.
source: Several of these genes we found to be required for daf-2's age-related improvement in learning and memory - namely dod-24, F08H9.4, C44B7.5, and alh-2 – were previously not associated with memory function.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' knowledge of the literature and their novel findings.

claim: The genes required for daf-2's extended memory with age are distinct from the set of upregulated Day 1 daf-2 vs daf-16;daf-2 genes.
source: Finally, these genes are distinct from the set of upregulated Day 1 daf-2 vs daf-16;daf-2 genes
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of Day 8 and Day 1 daf-2 vs daf-16;daf-2 differentially expressed genes shown in Figure 4a.

claim: An average of 47,233,119 counted reads per sample were obtained from Day 8 neuron RNA-seq.
source: We obtained an average of 47,233,119 counted reads per sample (Supplementary file 5)
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by data in Supplementary file 5.

claim: 16,488 coding and non-coding genes were detected in Day 8 neuron RNA-seq samples.
source: and detected the expression of 16,488 coding and non-coding genes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1e).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1e.

claim: A large fraction of the downregulated genes in Day 8 daf-2 vs daf-16;daf-2 neurons are 'nematode-specific peptide family' (nspc-) genes of unknown function.
source: A large fraction of the downregulated genes in Day 8 daf-2 vs daf-16;daf-2 neurons are 'nematode-specific peptide family' (nspc-) genes of unknown function (Figure 3f).
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of the downregulated genes shown in Figure 3f.

claim: Comparison of the daf-2 vs daf-16;daf-2 differential transcriptional changes in Day 8 whole worms and Day 8 neurons reveal shared (174 genes) and neuron-specific gene expression changes (396 genes).
source: comparison of the daf-2 vs daf-16;daf-2 differential transcriptional changes in Day 8 whole worms and Day 8 neurons reveal shared (174 genes) and neuron-specific gene expression changes (396 genes; dod-24, srh-2, lin-42, etc.) (Figure 3h, Figure 3—figure supplement 2c).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3h and Figure 3—figure supplement 2c.

claim: About a third of the daf-2-upregulated genes were shared between the daf-2 vs daf-16;daf-2 analysis and the daf-2 vs N2 analysis (338 genes).
source: We found that about a third of the daf-2-upregulated genes were shared between the daf-2 vs daf-16;daf-2 analysis and the daf-2 vs N2 analysis (338 genes) (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: The daf-2-maintained genes that are specific to the daf-2 vs N2 comparison are bZIP transcription factors and proteasome components.
source: Of the unshared genes, the daf-2-maintained genes that are specific to the daf-2 vs N2 comparison are bZIP transcription factors, including zip-5, zip-4, atf-2, and proteasome components (Figure 3—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3D.

claim: Some of the Day 8 daf-2 vs wild-type or daf-16;daf-2 upregulated genes are also Class 1 DAF-16-dependent genes.
source: Some of the Day 8 daf-2 vs wild-type or daf-16;daf-2 upregulated genes are also Class 1 DAF-16-dependent genes (Murphy et al., 2003) (sod-3, hsp-12.3, fat-5, and mtl-1, hil-1, and dao-2).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison with previously published Class 1 genes (Murphy et al., 2003).

claim: Many more genes were differentially expressed in Day 8 daf-2 vs daf-16;daf-2 neurons compared to Day 1 data.
source: However, many more genes were differentially expressed in Day 8 daf-2 vs daf-16;daf-2 neurons from our Day 1 data (Kaletsky et al., 2016; Figure 4a, Figure 3—figure supplement 2d).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of Day 8 and Day 1 data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: daf-2 worms are susceptible to RNA interference, including in neurons.
source: daf-2 worms, including neurons, are susceptible to RNA interference (Kaletsky et al., 2016; Wang, 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kaletsky et al., 2016 and Wang, 2004.

claim: alh-2 and F08H9.4 are only expressed in neurons and the cephalic sheath cell.
source: however, alh-2 and F08H9.4 were reported to only be expressed in neurons and the cephalic sheath cell (Kaletsky et al., 2018)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kaletsky et al., 2018.

claim: C44B7.5 and dod-24 were not upregulated in daf-2 in the whole-worm analysis.
source: and C44B7.5 and dod-24, while expressed more broadly, were not upregulated in daf-2 in the whole-worm analysis (Figure 3f)
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3f.

claim: dod-24 is one of the original Class 2 daf-2-downregulated genes from whole-animal analyses.
source: In fact, dod-24 is one of the original Class 2 daf-2-downregulated genes from whole-animal analyses
evidence: The claim is based on previous whole-animal analyses (Murphy et al., 2003).

claim: dod-24's increase in expression is specifically in neurons.
source: In fact, dod-24 is one of the original Class 2 daf-2-downregulated genes from whole-animal analyses, suggesting that dod-24's increase in expression is specifically in neurons
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that dod-24 is downregulated in whole-worm daf-2 but upregulated in daf-2 neurons.

claim: Sequencing many biological repeats of aging neurons to high depth with ribosomal RNA depletion allowed detection of a larger number of genes compared to other neuron-related bulk and single-cell sequencing profiles.
source: Sequencing many biological repeats of aging neurons to high depth with ribosomal RNA depletion allowed us to detect a larger number of genes compared to other neuron-related bulk and single-cell sequencing profiles (Wang et al., 2022)
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison with Wang et al., 2022 and the sequencing depth data.

claim: The sequencing results uncovered genes previously not known to be expressed in neurons that remained undetected in other datasets.
source: Notably, our sequencing results uncovered genes previously not known to be expressed in neurons that remained undetected in other datasets.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of the current dataset with other published datasets.

claim: The involvement of known neuronal genes in the aging process was revealed, such as ins-6 and srd-23.
source: Moreover, we revealed the involvement of known neuronal genes in the aging process, such as ins-6 and srd-23.
evidence: The claim is supported by the RNA-seq data showing changes in ins-6 and srd-23 expression with age.

claim: dod-24 has been shown to be an innate immunity gene upregulated during pathogen infection.
source: Functionally, it has been shown to be an innate immunity gene upregulated during pathogen infection (Shapira et al., 2006; Eckl et al., 2017; Mack et al., 2022)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Shapira et al., 2006; Eckl et al., 2017; and Mack et al., 2022.

claim: Whole-body reduction of dod-24 has been shown to extend the lifespan of wild-type animals.
source: and its whole-body reduction has been shown to extend the lifespan of wild-type animals (Murphy et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Murphy et al., 2003.

claim: dod-24 is beneficial in the nervous system and required for daf-2's extended learning and memory in aged worms.
source: However, here we find that dod-24 is beneficial in the nervous system and required for daf-2's extended learning and memory in aged worms.
evidence: The claim is supported by the RNAi knockdown experiments shown in Figure 4d-e.

claim: The Day 8 daf-2 vs daf-16;daf-2 neuronal differentially-expressed genes differ from the neuronal Day 1 daf-2 vs daf-16;daf-2 dataset.
source: We found that the Day 8 daf-2 vs daf-16;daf-2 neuronal differentially-expressed genes that we have newly discovered here differ from the neuronal Day 1 daf-2 vs daf-16;daf-2 dataset we previously obtained (Kaletsky et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of the current Day 8 data with previously published Day 1 data (Kaletsky et al., 2016), as shown in Figure 4a.

claim: Day 8 differentially-expressed genes are not canonical neuronal genes, such as receptors and ion channels.
source: These Day 8 differentially-expressed genes are not canonical neuronal genes, such as receptors and ion channels; instead, there are more metabolic and proteolytic genes whose protein orthologs have been shown to be neuroprotective.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of the Day 8 differentially expressed genes and their functional categories.

claim: daf-2 may enhance neuron's resilience to the accumulation of harm and take a more active approach to combat aging.
source: These results indicate that instead of simply mimicking a young state, daf-2 may enhance neuron's resilience to the accumulation of harm and take a more active approach to combat aging.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that Day 8 daf-2 upregulates stress response and neuroprotective genes that are different from Day 1.

claim: daf-2's extended memory maintenance may require different mechanisms than function in young animals.
source: These changes suggest that daf-2's extended memory maintenance may require different mechanisms than function in young animals
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that Day 8 and Day 1 daf-2 upregulated genes differ.

claim: daf-2 may maintain neuronal function not just by retaining a youthful transcriptome, but also by increasing the expression of genes that promote resilience.
source: daf-2 may maintain neuronal function not just by retaining a youthful transcriptome, but also by increasing the expression of genes that promote resilience, such as stress-response genes and proteolysis inhibitors.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that daf-2 upregulates stress response and proteolysis inhibitor genes with age.

claim: The downregulation of utx-1 decreases methylation on the daf-2 gene, thus increasing DAF-16's nuclear localization, mimicking a daf-2 mutation.
source: The loss of utx-1 decreases methylation on the daf-2 gene, thus increasing DAF-16's nuclear localization, mimicking a daf-2 mutation (Jin et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Jin et al., 2011.

claim: Certain insulin-like peptides have been linked to neuronal activities.
source: Notably, certain insulin-like peptides have been linked to neuronal activities, such as the regulation of aversive learning by the two antagonistic peptides ins-6 and ins-7 (Chen et al., 2013), and reduced long-term learning and memory by ins-22 RNAi (Lakhina et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2013 and Lakhina et al., 2015.
